section.heading: 11.4. The Comparison Tests
section.paragraph: In the comparison tests the idea is to compare a given series with a series that is known to be convergent or divergent. If two series have only positive terms, we can compare corresponding terms directly to see which are larger (the Direct Comparison Test) or we can investigate the limit of the ratios of corresponding terms (the Limit Comparison Test).
section.heading: The Direct Comparison Test
section.paragraph: Let’s consider the two series
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n} + 1}$$
and
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n}}$$

The second series $$\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}1 \slash 2^{n}$$ is a geometric series with $$a = \frac{1}{2}$$ and $$r = \frac{1}{2}$$ and is therefore convergent. Since these series are so similar, we may have the feeling that the first series must converge also. In fact, it does. The inequality

shows that the series $$\Sigma 1/\left( 2^{n} + 1 \right)$$ has smaller terms than those of the geometric series $$\Sigma 1/2^{n}$$ and therefore all its partial sums are also smaller than $$1$$ (the sum of the geometric series). This means that its partial sums form a bounded increasing sequence, which is convergent. It also follows that the sum of the series is less than the sum of the geometric series:
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n} + 1} < 1$$

Similar reasoning can be used to prove the following test, which applies only to series whose terms are positive. The first part says that if we have a series whose terms are smaller than those of a known convergent series, then our series is also convergent. The second part says that if we start with a series whose terms are larger than those of a known divergent series, then it too is divergent.

note.title: The Direct Comparison Test
note.heading: The Direct Comparison Test
note.paragraph: Suppose that $$\sum a_{n}$$ and $$\sum b_{n}$$ are series with positive terms.

list.item: (i) If $$\sum b_{n}$$ is convergent and $$a_{n} \leqslant b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , then $$\sum a_{n}$$ is also convergent.
(ii) If $$\sum b_{n}$$ is divergent and $$a_{n} \geqslant b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , then $$\sum a_{n}$$ is also divergent.

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof

list.item: (i) Let $$s_{n} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}a_{i}} t_{n} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}b_{i}} t = {\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}}$$ Since both series have positive terms, the sequences $$\left\{ s_{n} \right\}$$ and $$\left\{ t_{n} \right\}$$ are increasing $$(s_{n + 1} = s_{n} + a_{n + 1} \geqslant s_{n})$$ . Also $$\left. t_{n}\rightarrow t \right.$$ , so $$t_{n} \leqslant t$$ for all $$n$$ . Since $${a_{i} \leqslant}b_{i}$$ , we have $${s_{n} \leqslant}t_{n}$$ . Thus $$s_{n} \leqslant t$$ for all $$n$$ . This means that $$\left\{ s_{n} \right\}$$ is increasing and bounded above and therefore converges by the Monotonic Sequence Theorem. Thus $$\sum a_{n}$$ converges.

(ii) If $$\sum b_{n}$$ is divergent, then $$\left. t_{n}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ (since $$\left\{ t_{n} \right\}$$ is increasing). But $$a_{i} \geqslant b_{i}$$ so $$s_{n} \geqslant t_{n}$$ . Thus $$\left. s_{n}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . Therefore $$\sum a_{n}$$ diverges.

note.paragraph: It is important to keep in mind the distinction between a sequence and a series. A sequence is a list of numbers, whereas a series is a sum. With every series $$\sum a_{n}$$ there are two associated sequences: the sequence $$\left\{ a_{n} \right\}$$ of terms and the sequence $$\left\{ s_{n} \right\}$$ of partial sums.

note.title: Standard Series for Use with the Comparison Tests
note.heading: Standard Series for Use with the Comparison Tests
note.paragraph: In using the Direct Comparison Test we must, of course, have some known series $$\sum b_{n}$$ for the purpose of comparison. Most of the time we use one of these series:

list.item: A $$\mathit{p}$$ -series [ $$\sum 1 \slash n^{p}$$ converges if $$p > 1$$ and diverges if $$p \leqslant 1$$ ; see (11.3.1)]
A geometric series [ $$\sum ar^{n - 1}$$ converges if $$|r| < 1$$ and diverges if $$\left| r \middle| \geqslant 1 \right.$$ ; see (11.2.4)]

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Determine whether the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{5}{2n^{2} + 4n + 3}$$ converges or diverges.
Solution For large $$n$$ the dominant term in the denominator is $$2n^{2}$$ , so we compare the given series with the series $$\sum{5 \slash {(2n^{2})}}$$ . Observe that
because the left side has a bigger denominator. (In the notation of the Direct Comparison Test, $$a_{n}$$ is the left side and $$b_{n}$$ is the right side.) We know that
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{5}{2n^{2}} = \frac{5}{2}\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}$$
is convergent because it’s a constant times a $$p$$ -series with $$p = 2 > 1$$ . Therefore
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{5}{2n^{2} + 4n + 3}$$
is convergent by part (i) of the Direct Comparison Test.

section.paragraph: Note Although the condition $$a_{n} \leqslant b_{n}$$ or $$a_{n} \geqslant b_{n}$$ in the Direct Comparison Test is given for all $$n$$ , we need verify only that it holds for $$n \geqslant N$$ , where $$N$$ is some fixed integer, because the convergence of a series is not affected by a finite number of terms. This is illustrated in the next example.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Test the series $$\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{\infty}\frac{\ln k}{k}$$ for convergence or divergence.
Solution We used the Integral Test to test this series in Example 11.3.4, but we can also test it by comparing it with the harmonic series. Observe that $$\ln k > 1$$ for $$k \geqslant 3$$ and so
$${\frac{\ln k}{k} > \frac{1}{k}} {k \geqslant 3}$$
We know that $$\sum 1 \slash k$$ is divergent ( $$p$$ -series with $$p = 1$$ ). Thus the given series is divergent by the Direct Comparison Test.

section.heading: Limit Comparison Test
section.paragraph: The Direct Comparison Test is conclusive only if the terms of the series being tested are smaller than those of a convergent series or larger than those of a divergent series. If the terms are larger than the terms of a convergent series or smaller than those of a divergent series, then the Direct Comparison Test doesn’t apply. Consider, for instance, the series
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n} - 1}$$
The inequality

is useless as far as the Direct Comparison Test is concerned because $$\sum b_{n} = \sum\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n}$$ is convergent and $$a_{n} > b_{n}$$ . Nonetheless, we have the feeling that $$\sum 1 \slash \left( 2^{n} - 1) \right.$$ ought to be convergent because it is very similar to the convergent geometric series $$\sum\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n}$$ . In such cases the following test can be used.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Test the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n} - 1}$$ for convergence or divergence.
Solution We use the Limit Comparison Test with
and obtain

$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1 \slash \left( {2^{n} - 1} \right)}{1 \slash 2^{n}} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2^{n}}{2^{n} - 1} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{1 - 1 \slash 2^{n}} = 1 > 0$$
Since this limit exists and $$\sum 1 \slash 2^{n}$$ is a convergent geometric series, the given series converges by the Limit Comparison Test.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Determine whether the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{2n^{2} + 3n}{\sqrt{5 + n^{5}}}$$ converges or diverges.
Solution The dominant part of the numerator is $$2n^{2}$$ and the dominant part of the denominator is $$\sqrt{n^{5}} = n^{5 \slash 2}$$ . This suggests taking

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2n^{2} + 3n}{\sqrt{5 + n^{5}}} \cdot \frac{n^{1 \slash 2}}{2} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2n^{5 \slash 2} + 3n^{3 \slash 2}}{2\sqrt{5 + n^{5}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2 + \frac{3}{n}}{2\sqrt{\frac{5}{n^{5}} + 1}} = \frac{2 + 0}{2\sqrt{0 + 1}} = 1} \end{array}$$
Since $$\sum b_{n} = 2\sum 1 \slash n^{1 \slash 2}$$ is divergent ( $$p$$ -series with $$p = \frac{1}{2} < 1)$$ , the given series diverges by the Limit Comparison Test.

section.paragraph: Notice that in testing many series we find a suitable comparison series $$\sum b_{n}$$ by keeping only the highest powers in the numerator and denominator.
section.heading: Estimating Sums
section.paragraph: If we have used the Direct Comparison Test to show that a series $$\sum a_{n}$$ converges by comparison with a series $$\sum b_{n}$$ , then we may be able to estimate the sum $$\sum a_{n}$$ by comparing remainders. As in Section 11.3, we consider the remainder
For the comparison series $$\sum b_{n}$$ we consider the corresponding remainder

Since $$a_{n} \leqslant b_{n}$$ for all $$n$$ , we have $$R_{n} \leqslant T_{n}$$ . If $$\sum b_{n}$$ is a $$p$$ -series, we can estimate its remainder $$T_{n}$$ as in Section 11.3. If $$\sum b_{n}$$ is a geometric series, then $$T_{n}$$ is the sum of a geometric series and we can sum it exactly (see Exercises 43 and 44). In either case we know that $$R_{n}$$ is smaller than $$T_{n}$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Use the sum of the first $$100$$ terms to approximate the sum of the series $$\sum 1 \slash \left( {n^{3} + 1} \right)$$ . Estimate the error involved in this approximation.
